# Descriptive analysis and model selection

This file follows `02_dta_cleaning.qmd`. We read the quarterly data built there and use it for descriptive analysis and model selection only; no data is built or modified here.

```{r}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(urca)       # ur.df() (ADF), ur.kpss() (KPSS)
library(forecast)   # nsdiffs()

clean_dir <- here("DTA_CLEAN")

# Quarterly data built in 02: headline CPI, the 4 blocks and the oil drivers
quarterly <- read_csv(file.path(clean_dir, "quarterly_data.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Logs x 100 of every series: a first difference is then (approximately)
# the quarterly change in %
quarterly <- quarterly %>%
  mutate(across(-date, ~ 100 * log(.x), .names = "l_{.col}"))

# Check: period covered, number of quarters, columns
range(quarterly$date)
nrow(quarterly)
names(quarterly)
```

# 1. Overview of the series

```{r}
# Readable names for the 5 series (headline + 4 blocks)
block_names <- c(l_cpi_total     = "Headline CPI",
                 l_cpi_oil       = "Oil products",
                 l_cpi_rent      = "Rents",
                 l_cpi_imp_xoil  = "Imported excl. oil",
                 l_cpi_dom_xrent = "Domestic excl. rents")

# Long format (one row per quarter and series), with the quarterly change
# (q-o-q) and the change over 4 quarters (y-o-y), both in %
inflation <- quarterly %>%
  select(date, all_of(names(block_names))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "series", values_to = "log_index") %>%
  group_by(series) %>%
  mutate(qoq = log_index - lag(log_index),
         yoy = log_index - lag(log_index, 4)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(series = factor(block_names[series], levels = block_names))

# Levels: trends and breaks
ggplot(inflation, aes(date, log_index)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ series, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "CPI blocks, 100 x log(index)", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Year-on-year inflation: the deflation episodes and the 2022 surge
ggplot(filter(inflation, !is.na(yoy)), aes(date, yoy)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ series, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Year-on-year inflation, in %", x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

1.  Two regimes. All blocks show high inflation from 1989 to 1993 (rents up to 10 %, headline about 6 %), and inflation remains below 3 % afterwards. Since the early 1990s differ clearly from the rest of the sample, we start the estimation sample in 2000.

2.  Deflation period. It is strongest in imported excl. oil: the level falls by about 12 % between 2011 and 2016 and y/y inflation reaches −5 % in 2012, reflecting the strong franc. Headline and domestic excl. rents are also slightly negative over 2012–2016 and in 2020.

3.  Seasonality in imported excl. oil between 2000 and about 2015, visible as a zig-zag in the level. It comes mainly from clothing and shoes, whose prices fall during the January and July sales. Sale prices are only recorded by the BFS since 2000, and the pattern weakens after about 2015. The seasonal pattern therefore changes over the sample, which we take into account in section 3.

4.  Rents rise smoothly, with no breaks and no seasonality. Growth is almost constant after 1995 and slower in 2010–2020.

5.  Oil products are very volatile, between −40 % and +35 % y/y, with falls in 2009, 2015 and 2020 and peaks in 2000, 2008 and 2022. For this reason we model this block separately, with Brent and the USD exchange rate as drivers.

6.  The 2021–2023 inflation episode is a common shock visible in every block, followed by a return to about 0–1.5 %.

# 2. Descriptive statistics

```{r}
# Sub-periods seen in the plots
inflation <- inflation %>%
  mutate(period = case_when(year(date) <= 1993 ~ "1988-1993 high inflation",
                            year(date) <= 2008 ~ "1994-2008 low inflation",
                            year(date) <= 2016 ~ "2009-2016 strong franc",
                            year(date) <= 2020 ~ "2017-2020",
                            TRUE               ~ "2021-2026 surge and fall"))

# Quarterly inflation (q-o-q, in %), whole sample from 2000
inflation %>%
  filter(year(date) >= 2000) %>%
  group_by(series) %>%
  summarise(quarters = sum(!is.na(qoq)),
            mean     = mean(qoq),
            sd       = sd(qoq),
            min      = min(qoq),
            max      = max(qoq),
            share_negative = mean(qoq < 0)) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2)))

# Mean year-on-year inflation (in %) by sub-period
inflation %>%
  filter(!is.na(yoy)) %>%
  group_by(series, period) %>%
  summarise(mean_yoy = round(mean(yoy), 2), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = mean_yoy) %>%
  as.data.frame()          # data.frame shows all columns
```

The blocks behave very differently, which supports modelling them separately. Oil products are the most volatile, with a standard deviation 23 times that of rents. Rents are stable and almost always rising (only 8 % of quarters are negative). Imported excl. oil falls more often than it rises.

Imported excl. oil has a negative average (−0.12 % per quarter). The second table shows that this comes from the strong-franc period 2009–2016 (−1.8 % y/y); in the other periods the average is close to zero or positive. An ARIMA with drift estimated from 2000 would carry this negative average into the forecast. We address this in model selection, either with a 2009–2016 dummy or without drift.

Imported excl. oil is also volatile for a non-energy block (sd 1.89), while its y/y inflation is much smoother. Most of the q-o-q volatility is therefore the seasonal pattern from sales, which we test in section 3.

Inflation in the early 1990s is four to five times higher than later in every block. We therefore start the estimation sample in 2000 rather than in 1988.

# 3. Seasonality

```{r}
# Seasonality test for one block on one sample: regress q-o-q inflation on
# quarter dummies; F-test H0 = "all quarters have the same mean inflation"
seasonal_test <- function(data) {
  fit <- lm(qoq ~ factor(quarter(date)), data = data)
  f   <- summary(fit)$fstatistic
  tibble(f_stat  = round(f[["value"]], 2),
         p_value = round(pf(f[["value"]], f[["numdf"]], f[["dendf"]], lower.tail = FALSE), 4),
         r2      = round(summary(fit)$r.squared, 2))
}

# Test on the sample from 2000, and on two halves to see if the pattern changed
seasonality <- inflation %>%
  filter(year(date) >= 2000, !is.na(qoq)) %>%
  mutate(sample = if_else(year(date) <= 2012, "2000-2012", "2013-2026"))

bind_rows(
  seasonality %>% mutate(sample = "2000-2026"),
  seasonality) %>%
  group_by(series, sample) %>%
  group_modify(~ seasonal_test(.x)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  as.data.frame()

# Mean q-o-q inflation by quarter: the seasonal pattern itself
seasonality %>%
  group_by(series, sample, q = paste0("Q", quarter(date))) %>%
  summarise(mean_qoq = round(mean(qoq), 2), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = q, values_from = mean_qoq) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

The blocks fall into three groups.

1.  Imported excl. oil is the most seasonal block. Quarter dummies explain about two thirds of its q-o-q inflation (R² = 0.67, F = 70). Prices fall in Q1 and Q3 and rise in Q2 and Q4, in line with the January and July sales. The pattern weakens strongly between the two halves: Q3 goes from −2.64 to −1.13 and Q4 from +1.84 to +0.23. This is consistent with the level plot and explains most of the q-o-q volatility found in section 2.

2.  Domestic excl. rents is also clearly seasonal (R² = 0.44), with a stable pattern. Q1 is about +0.5 % in both halves, as many prices are adjusted at the start of the year (tariffs, administered prices, services). Only Q4 changes, from about 0 to −0.33.

3.  Rents and oil products show little seasonality. For rents the test never rejects (p = 0.59 on the full sample, 0.93 after 2012). For oil it rejects only on the full sample at 5 % (p = 0.01, R² = 0.10); Q2 is positive, in line with the spring driving season, but small relative to its volatility (sd 6.5).

Headline CPI is seasonal (R² = 0.43), mainly through imported and domestic goods, and its seasonality weakens together with the imported pattern (R² 0.62 → 0.39).

For model selection, we include a seasonal term for imported and domestic goods, but not for rents and oil. For imported goods, fixed quarter dummies estimated from 2000 would carry the strong early-2000s pattern into the forecast. We therefore consider a seasonal AR term or a seasonal difference, which can adapt to a changing pattern (sections 4 and 5). Although the seasonality largely cancels in y-o-y inflation, it still has to be modelled in the q-o-q models.

# 4. Stationarity

```{r unit-roots}
# Series to test, from 2000Q1: the 4 blocks and the 3 oil-ECM variables
test_vars <- c("l_cpi_oil", "l_cpi_rent", "l_cpi_imp_xoil", "l_cpi_dom_xrent",
               "l_brent_usd", "l_chf_per_usd", "l_brent_chf")

sample_2000 <- quarterly %>% filter(year(date) >= 2000)
qtr <- factor(quarter(sample_2000$date))

# Remove the seasonal pattern before testing (subtract the mean of each
# quarter): the ADF and KPSS tests assume no seasonality, and a seasonal
# zig-zag makes them unreliable.
deseason <- function(x, q) x - ave(x, q) + mean(x)

# ADF:  H0 = unit root (non-stationary). Reject if stat < 5% critical value.
# KPSS: H0 = stationary.                 Reject if stat > 5% critical value.
# Levels: with constant and trend. First differences: with constant only.
# ADF lags chosen by BIC (max 4 = one year).
unit_root_tests <- function(x, q) {
  lvl <- deseason(x, q)
  dif <- deseason(diff(x), q[-1])
  adf_l  <- ur.df(lvl, type = "trend", lags = 4, selectlags = "BIC")
  adf_d  <- ur.df(dif, type = "drift", lags = 4, selectlags = "BIC")
  kpss_l <- ur.kpss(lvl, type = "tau")
  kpss_d <- ur.kpss(dif, type = "mu")
  tibble(adf_level   = adf_l@teststat[1],  adf_level_cv5  = adf_l@cval[1, "5pct"],
         kpss_level  = kpss_l@teststat,    kpss_level_cv5 = kpss_l@cval[1, "5pct"],
         adf_diff    = adf_d@teststat[1],  adf_diff_cv5   = adf_d@cval[1, "5pct"],
         kpss_diff   = kpss_d@teststat,    kpss_diff_cv5  = kpss_d@cval[1, "5pct"],
         # number of seasonal differences needed (OCSB test, raw series)
         seasonal_diffs = nsdiffs(ts(x, frequency = 4), test = "ocsb"))
}

unit_roots <- map(test_vars, \(v) unit_root_tests(sample_2000[[v]], qtr)) %>%
  list_rbind() %>%
  mutate(series = test_vars, .before = 1) %>%
  mutate(level_stationary = adf_level < adf_level_cv5 & kpss_level < kpss_level_cv5,
         diff_stationary  = adf_diff  < adf_diff_cv5  & kpss_diff  < kpss_diff_cv5,
         across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 2)))

unit_roots %>% as.data.frame()
```

All series are I(1): non-stationary in levels and stationary in first differences. We therefore use d = 1 for the three ARIMA blocks, i.e. we model quarterly inflation rather than the price level, as is standard for price indices.

Domestic excl. rents is a borderline case in levels: the ADF test rejects the unit root (−3.63 \< −3.43), while the KPSS test rejects stationarity. Given this conflict, we difference the series. Not differencing an I(1) series leads to biased long-horizon forecasts, while an unnecessary difference has a smaller cost.

Imported and domestic goods are only marginally stationary in differences (−2.97 and −2.92 vs −2.88). This is consistent with the plots, where inflation stays away from its mean for long periods (strong-franc years, 2022 surge). In the ARIMA models this is captured by AR terms, and possibly by a 2009–2016 dummy.

For imported excl. oil, the OCSB test indicates one seasonal difference. This is consistent with section 3, where the seasonal pattern weakens over time. For this block we therefore consider two specifications: a seasonal difference (D = 1), or a seasonal AR term with d = 1.

Oil products, Brent and the exchange rate are all I(1), which is the condition for testing cointegration and estimating an ECM.

# 5. Model selection: ARIMA blocks

```{r arima-selection}
# The three ARIMA blocks, as quarterly time series from 2000Q1
arima_vars <- c(Rents                  = "l_cpi_rent",
                `Imported excl. oil`   = "l_cpi_imp_xoil",
                `Domestic excl. rents` = "l_cpi_dom_xrent")

to_ts <- function(v) ts(sample_2000[[v]], start = c(2000, 1), frequency = 4)

# Candidate models: ARIMA(p,1,q)(P,0,0)[4] with drift,
# p = 0..3, q = 0..2, P = 0 (no seasonal term) or 1 (seasonal AR)
grid <- expand_grid(p = 0:3, q = 0:2, P = 0:1)

fit_grid <- function(y) {
  pmap(grid, \(p, q, P) {
    fit <- tryCatch(Arima(y, order = c(p, 1, q), seasonal = c(P, 0, 0),
                          include.drift = TRUE),
                    error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(fit)) return(NULL)
    tibble(p = p, q = q, P = P,
           aicc = fit$aicc, bic = fit$bic,
           # Ljung-Box on residuals, 8 lags (2 years): H0 = no autocorrelation
           lb_p = Box.test(residuals(fit), lag = 8, type = "Ljung-Box",
                           fitdf = p + q + P)$p.value)
  }) %>% list_rbind()
}

arima_grid <- imap(arima_vars, \(v, name) fit_grid(to_ts(v)) %>% mutate(block = name)) %>%
  list_rbind() %>%
  relocate(block)

# Best 3 models by BIC in each block
arima_grid %>%
  group_by(block) %>%
  slice_min(bic, n = 3) %>%
  mutate(across(c(aicc, bic, lb_p), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  as.data.frame()

# Re-estimate the best model by BIC of each block and show its coefficients
best <- arima_grid %>% group_by(block) %>% slice_min(bic, n = 1) %>% ungroup()

best_fits <- pmap(best, \(block, p, q, P, ...) {
  Arima(to_ts(arima_vars[[block]]), order = c(p, 1, q), seasonal = c(P, 0, 0),
        include.drift = TRUE)
}) %>% set_names(best$block)

imap(best_fits, \(fit, name) {
  tibble(block = name, term = names(coef(fit)),
         estimate = coef(fit), se = sqrt(diag(fit$var.coef))) %>%
    mutate(t = estimate / se)
}) %>%
  list_rbind() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

**Rents: ARIMA(1,1,1)(1,0,0) with drift.** All coefficients are significant and the residuals show no autocorrelation (Ljung-Box p = 0.74). The drift of 0.36 % per quarter implies long-run rent inflation of about 1.4 % per year. The seasonal AR term is significant (0.27) although section 3 found no seasonal means: rent inflation is related to the same quarter of the previous year, consistent with yearly rent adjustments (e.g. after reference-rate changes). The three best models are close in BIC.

**Imported excl. oil: ARIMA(2,1,1)(1,0,0) with drift.**

- The drift is negative (−0.14 % per quarter) and not significant. It reflects the strong-franc period and would imply steadily falling import prices at long horizons. We compare a model without drift and a model with a 2009–2016 dummy.
- ar1 = −0.70 and ma1 = +0.74 nearly cancel, which suggests a common factor and a possibly over-parameterised model.
- The seasonal difference suggested by the OCSB test cannot be compared by BIC, since it changes the data being fitted. We compare it by out-of-sample forecast accuracy.

**Domestic excl. rents: ARIMA(0,1,0)(1,0,0) with drift.** Inflation depends only on the same quarter of the previous year (sar1 = 0.73), in line with the stable Q1 pattern of section 3. The residuals pass the Ljung-Box test only marginally (p = 0.11). The second-best model, ARIMA(1,1,0)(1,0,0), has a very similar BIC (30.2 vs 30.0), a lower AICc and cleaner residuals (p = 0.62), so we keep it as an alternative. The drift of 0.15 % per quarter (about 0.6 % per year) is borderline significant (t = 1.8) and also reduced by the strong-franc years.

BIC provides the first selection. The remaining choices (imported drift or dummy, seasonal difference, domestic specification) can be assessed with the out-of-sample comparison of section 8.

# 6. Oil products: cointegration and ECM

```{r oil-ecm}
# Oil block variables (logs x 100), from 2000Q1
oil <- sample_2000 %>%
  transmute(date,
            oil   = l_cpi_oil,        # CPI oil products
            brent = l_brent_usd,      # Brent, USD per barrel
            usd   = l_chf_per_usd,    # CHF per USD
            trend = row_number())     # linear trend (1, 2, 3, ...)

# --- 1. Long-run relation (static regression in levels) ---
# Without and with a linear trend; the trend captures slowly rising
# taxes and margins (mineral oil tax, CO2 levy since 2008)
lr_const <- lm(oil ~ brent + usd,         data = oil)
lr_trend <- lm(oil ~ brent + usd + trend, data = oil)
summary(lr_const)$coefficients
summary(lr_trend)$coefficients

# --- 2. Engle-Granger test: is the long-run residual stationary? ---
# ADF on the residuals, no constant (they have mean 0 by construction).
# Critical values are NOT the usual ADF ones: the residuals come from an
# estimated regression. MacKinnon (2010), 3 variables, 5% level:
# -3.74 (constant), -4.10 (constant + trend).
eg_stat <- function(fit) {
  ur.df(residuals(fit), type = "none", lags = 4, selectlags = "BIC")@teststat[1]
}
tibble(long_run = c("constant", "constant + trend"),
       eg_stat  = c(eg_stat(lr_const), eg_stat(lr_trend)),
       cv_5pct  = c(-3.74, -4.10)) %>%
  mutate(cointegrated = eg_stat < cv_5pct)

# --- 3. Johansen trace test (system approach, robustness check) ---
# r = number of cointegrating relations; reject "r = 0" if stat > critical value.
# K = 2 lags in levels, trend in the cointegrating relation.
# Same call as in 04_model_estimation.R, so both report the same statistic.
johansen <- ca.jo(oil[, c("oil", "brent", "usd")], type = "trace",
                  ecdet = "trend", K = 2, spec = "transitory")
cbind(stat = round(johansen@teststat, 2), johansen@cval)

# --- 4. Same effect of Brent and of the exchange rate? ---
# If b_brent = b_usd, only Brent in CHF matters. Re-parametrised so that the
# coefficient on usd is b_usd - b_brent: H0 = this coefficient is 0.
summary(lm(oil ~ I(brent + usd) + usd + trend, data = oil))$coefficients["usd", ]

# --- 5. ECM lag selection ---
# d_oil_t = c + alpha * ect_(t-1) + b * d_brent_t + g * d_usd_t
#           + L lags of d_oil, d_brent and d_usd
# ect = residual of the long-run relation with trend (deviation from equilibrium)
ecm_data <- oil %>%
  mutate(ect     = residuals(lr_trend),
         ect_l1  = lag(ect),
         d_oil   = oil   - lag(oil),
         d_brent = brent - lag(brent),
         d_usd   = usd   - lag(usd))

for (i in 1:4) {
  ecm_data[[paste0("d_oil_l",   i)]] <- lag(ecm_data$d_oil,   i)
  ecm_data[[paste0("d_brent_l", i)]] <- lag(ecm_data$d_brent, i)
  ecm_data[[paste0("d_usd_l",   i)]] <- lag(ecm_data$d_usd,   i)
}

# All models on the same sample (lose the first 5 quarters), so BIC is comparable
ecm_sample <- ecm_data %>% slice(6:n())

ecm_formula <- function(L) {
  lags <- if (L == 0) NULL else paste0(c("d_oil_l", "d_brent_l", "d_usd_l"), rep(1:L, each = 3))
  reformulate(c("ect_l1", "d_brent", "d_usd", lags), response = "d_oil")
}

map(0:4, \(L) {
  fit <- lm(ecm_formula(L), data = ecm_sample)
  tibble(lags    = L,
         bic     = BIC(fit),
         alpha   = coef(fit)[["ect_l1"]],
         t_alpha = summary(fit)$coefficients["ect_l1", "t value"],
         r2      = summary(fit)$r.squared,
         lb_p    = Box.test(residuals(fit), lag = 8, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
}) %>%
  list_rbind() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 3)))

# Chosen ECM (1 lag), estimated on all available quarters
ecm_fit <- lm(ecm_formula(1), data = ecm_data)
round(summary(ecm_fit)$coefficients, 3)
```

**Long-run relation.** The result depends on the trend.

- With a constant only, the USD coefficient has the wrong sign (−0.09) and is not significant, and the Engle-Granger test does not reject (−2.85 vs −3.74).
- With a trend, all coefficients are significant: Brent 0.43, USD 0.61, trend 0.42 % per quarter (about 1.7 % per year). The Engle-Granger test rejects (−5.30 vs −4.10).

We interpret the trend economically: Swiss fuel prices include per-litre taxes (mineral oil tax, CO2 levy since 2008) and distribution margins that rise over time independently of crude prices. These components also explain why the Brent elasticity is below 1.

**Johansen test.** The trace test does not reject r = 0 (37.98 \< 42.44 at 5 % and \< 39.06 at 10 %), so the two tests disagree. We keep the ECM because:

- the Johansen test has low power with 3 variables, a trend and about 105 quarters;
- we need a single relation with oil products as the dependent variable, which corresponds to the Engle-Granger setting;
- the adjustment coefficient of the ECM is strongly significant, which is itself evidence of cointegration.

The statistic is the same as in `04_model_estimation.R`. Adding quarter dummies (`season = 4`) gives 37.80, with the same conclusion.

**Brent vs. exchange rate.** Equal elasticities are rejected (t = 4.09 on b_usd − b_brent = 0.19), so we keep Brent and the USD rate as separate variables rather than using Brent in CHF. The higher USD elasticity is likely partly due to the trend and the long appreciation of the franc moving together, and should be interpreted with caution.

**Short-run dynamics.** BIC selects 1 lag (515 vs 527 with no lags), and the residuals show no autocorrelation (Ljung-Box p = 0.73).

- α = −0.39 (t = −4.3): about 40 % of a deviation from the long-run equilibrium is corrected each quarter (half-life of about 1.4 quarters).
- Pass-through is fast: within the same quarter, Brent passes 0.31 and the USD rate 0.54, compared with long-run elasticities of 0.43 and 0.61. The lagged Brent term (0.10) is significant.
- The lagged oil and USD terms are not significant; we keep them so that all three variables have the same lag structure.

The ECM is a conditional model: forecasts of oil products require paths for Brent and the USD rate. In the recursive evaluation, both steps (long run and ECM) are re-estimated in each window, as done by `fit_ecm()` in `R/models.R`.


# 7. Diagnostic tests

```{r diagnostics}
library(tseries)    # jarque.bera.test()

# Residuals of the chosen models: the 3 ARIMA blocks and the oil ECM
model_resid <- c(map(best_fits, residuals), list(`Oil (ECM)` = residuals(ecm_fit)))

# Jarque-Bera: H0 = normal residuals
# Ljung-Box on squared residuals: H0 = constant variance (no ARCH)
imap(model_resid, \(e, name) {
  tibble(model  = name,
         jb_p   = jarque.bera.test(e)$p.value,
         arch_p = Box.test(e^2, lag = 4, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
}) %>%
  list_rbind() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

No model shows changing variance (all ARCH p > 0.4). The oil ECM residuals are normal. The residuals of the three ARIMA models are not, because of a few outlier quarters: the electricity tariff increase in 2023Q1 for domestic goods, and the franc peak in 2011Q4 for imported goods. This does not bias the point forecasts, but the prediction intervals of these blocks are less reliable.

# 8. Forecast evaluation

```{r evaluation}
# --- Set-up ---
# Pseudo out-of-sample: at each origin (2015Q4, 2016Q1, ...) we re-estimate
# every model on the data up to that quarter only, forecast 1 to 4 quarters
# ahead and compare with what actually happened.
first_origin <- which(sample_2000$date == as.Date("2015-10-01"))
n_obs        <- nrow(sample_2000)
origins      <- first_origin:(n_obs - 1)
h_max        <- 4

# --- 1. ARIMA blocks: chosen model vs AR(1) ---
# AR(1) benchmark = AR(1) on q-o-q inflation = ARIMA(1,1,0) with drift.
# Both forecast the log level; at h = 4 the error is the error on the
# change over 4 quarters, i.e. on y-o-y inflation.
arima_errors <- imap(arima_vars, \(v, name) {
  y   <- to_ts(v)
  ord <- arimaorder(best_fits[[name]])
  map(origins, \(t) {
    y_in <- window(y, end = time(y)[t])
    n_h  <- min(h_max, n_obs - t)
    f_model <- forecast(Arima(y_in, order = ord[1:3], seasonal = ord[4:6],
                              include.drift = TRUE), h = n_h)$mean
    f_ar1   <- forecast(Arima(y_in, order = c(1, 1, 0), include.drift = TRUE), h = n_h)$mean
    tibble(block = name, origin = sample_2000$date[t], h = 1:n_h,
           e_model = y[t + 1:n_h] - as.numeric(f_model),
           e_ar1   = y[t + 1:n_h] - as.numeric(f_ar1))
  }) %>% list_rbind()
}) %>% list_rbind()

# --- 2. Oil ECM vs AR(1) ---
# The ECM needs future Brent and USD. We assume no change after the origin
# (random walk for the drivers), which is what we could have assumed in real time.
ecm_forecast <- function(t, h) {
  train <- oil %>% slice(1:t)
  lr    <- lm(oil ~ brent + usd + trend, data = train)
  d     <- train %>%
    mutate(ect_l1     = lag(residuals(lr)),
           d_oil      = oil - lag(oil),     d_oil_l1   = lag(d_oil),
           d_brent    = brent - lag(brent), d_brent_l1 = lag(d_brent),
           d_usd      = usd - lag(usd),     d_usd_l1   = lag(d_usd))
  b     <- coef(lm(ecm_formula(1), data = d))
  last  <- tail(d, 1)
  level <- last$oil
  ect   <- residuals(lr)[t]
  d_oil_prev <- last$d_oil; d_brent_prev <- last$d_brent; d_usd_prev <- last$d_usd
  out <- numeric(h)
  for (i in 1:h) {
    # d_brent = d_usd = 0 in the forecast quarters
    d_oil <- b[["(Intercept)"]] + b[["ect_l1"]] * ect + b[["d_oil_l1"]] * d_oil_prev +
             b[["d_brent_l1"]] * d_brent_prev + b[["d_usd_l1"]] * d_usd_prev
    level <- level + d_oil
    ect   <- level - predict(lr, newdata = tibble(brent = last$brent, usd = last$usd,
                                                  trend = last$trend + i))
    d_oil_prev <- d_oil; d_brent_prev <- 0; d_usd_prev <- 0
    out[i] <- level
  }
  out
}

y_oil <- ts(oil$oil, start = c(2000, 1), frequency = 4)
oil_errors <- map(origins, \(t) {
  n_h   <- min(h_max, n_obs - t)
  f_ecm <- ecm_forecast(t, n_h)
  f_ar1 <- forecast(Arima(window(y_oil, end = time(y_oil)[t]), order = c(1, 1, 0),
                          include.drift = TRUE), h = n_h)$mean
  tibble(block = "Oil (ECM)", origin = sample_2000$date[t], h = 1:n_h,
         e_model = oil$oil[t + 1:n_h] - f_ecm,
         e_ar1   = oil$oil[t + 1:n_h] - as.numeric(f_ar1))
}) %>% list_rbind()

# --- 3. Accuracy: RMSE, ratio to AR(1), Diebold-Mariano test ---
# ratio < 1: our model beats the AR(1).
# DM test: H0 = both models are equally accurate (squared errors).
oos_errors <- bind_rows(arima_errors, oil_errors)

oos_errors %>%
  filter(h %in% c(1, 4)) %>%
  group_by(block, h) %>%
  summarise(n          = n(),
            rmse_model = sqrt(mean(e_model^2)),
            rmse_ar1   = sqrt(mean(e_ar1^2)),
            ratio      = rmse_model / rmse_ar1,
            dm_p       = dm.test(e_model, e_ar1, h = first(h), power = 2)$p.value,
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.double), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

We evaluate the models by pseudo out-of-sample forecasting from 2015Q4, re-estimating each model every quarter on the data available at the time. About 40 forecasts per block are compared with an AR(1) benchmark.

- **Imported and domestic goods** outperform the AR(1) one quarter ahead: errors are 30–40 % smaller, and the difference is significant (DM p = 0.002 and 0.016). The gain comes from the seasonal term, which the AR(1) does not include. Four quarters ahead our models remain better (ratios 0.88 and 0.94), but not significantly, as the seasonal pattern largely cancels over a full year.
- **Oil products (ECM)** are forecast better than with the AR(1) at both horizons (ratios 0.92 and 0.95), but not significantly. Oil prices are difficult to forecast, and we assume constant Brent and USD after each origin.
- **Rents** show no gain over the AR(1): both models perform equally, consistent with the absence of seasonality in rents.

With about 40 forecasts the DM test has limited power, and the evaluation window includes the 2021–2023 inflation surge, which none of the models anticipated.
